"Legendary" comes from the word legend — a story, usually about an extraordinary person or event, that gets passed down through generations and becomes larger than life in the telling. When something is called legendary, it carries that same quality: it is so remarkable, so impressive, or so famous that it has risen to the level of a story people keep telling long after the fact.

Sense 1: Belonging to or described in legend

This is the original, more literal meaning. It describes someone or something that exists in ancient stories, myths, or folklore — not necessarily proven by history, but deeply embedded in human storytelling tradition.

  • The legendary King Arthur ruled over Camelot. (Arthur is a figure from legend and folklore, not a historically verified king.)
  • The Minotaur is a legendary creature from Greek mythology. (It is a being found in ancient legends.)
  • Legendary heroes like Hercules were believed to have superhuman strength.

In this sense, "legendary" often has a slight haze of the unknown about it — the figure or story may not be fully real, but it has been told and retold with such power and admiration that it has taken on a life of its own.

Sense 2: So famous and extraordinary that the person or thing has become almost like a legend

This is the more common modern meaning. Here, the person or thing being described is real — not from folklore — but their greatness, fame, or impact is so enormous that people speak of them the way you'd speak of a legendary hero. They have transcended ordinary fame and entered a kind of mythical territory.

  • Muhammad Ali was a legendary boxer. (He was real, but his skills and personality were so extraordinary that his reputation has taken on an almost mythical quality.)
  • The Beatles gave a legendary performance at Shea Stadium. (The performance was so stunning that it has been talked about in awe for decades.)
  • She has a legendary reputation for getting things done under pressure.

In this sense, "legendary" always implies two things at once: extraordinary greatness and enduring fame — the kind of fame that doesn't fade, that gets passed from person to person almost like a story.

The reason the word stretches naturally from Sense 1 to Sense 2 is this: in both cases, something has risen above the ordinary to the point where it lives in people's minds as a story worth telling and retelling. Whether it's King Arthur or Muhammad Ali, the word signals: this is not average; this is the kind of thing people talk about long after it's gone.
The feel and connotations of the word

"Legendary" is not a neutral word — it is almost always a word of admiration and awe. When you call something legendary, you are saying it belongs in a category far above the ordinary. It carries these qualities:

  • Greatness: Whatever is called legendary is exceptional, not just good.
  • Endurance: The fame or impact has lasted. A one-day wonder isn't legendary. Something legendary has stood the test of time — or at least feels like it will.
  • Larger-than-life quality: The word has a slightly dramatic, almost epic feel to it. Legends are bigger than real life. So is something legendary.
  • Wide recognition: Even if you weren't there, you've heard about it. Legendary things are known beyond the people who witnessed them firsthand.

Famous simply means well-known. A celebrity can be famous without being legendary. "Legendary" implies a higher, more awe-inspiring level of fame — the kind where people speak the name with reverence.

Infamous means well-known for something bad. "Legendary" is almost never used in a negative sense — it leans strongly positive.

Iconic means widely recognized as a symbol of something. It's about being a powerful symbol or image. "Legendary" is more about greatness of deed, skill, or story.

Historic means significant in history, having made an impact on events. "Legendary" is more personal, more emotional — it's about admiration and the story that gets told, not just the factual impact.

Mythical means imaginary or fictional, not real. "Legendary" can describe real people. You'd say Muhammad Ali was legendary, not mythical. But a dragon is mythical. The overlap is that both words have a "larger than life" quality — mythical things don't exist, while legendary things exist (or existed) but have been elevated to near-mythical status through their extraordinary nature.

You will see "legendary" used in several recurring patterns:

  • Before a person's name or role: the legendary singer, legendary coach Vince Lombardi, a legendary warrior
  • Before a performance or achievement: a legendary concert, his legendary speech, a legendary season
  • To describe someone's reputation or skill: Her patience is legendary, His cooking is legendary in our family
  • With words like "status" or "proportions": reached legendary status, a scandal of legendary proportions

In casual conversation, especially among younger speakers, "legendary" is sometimes used hyperbolically — meaning extremely impressive or unforgettable, even for smaller things:

  • That goal he scored was legendary.
  • Last night's party was absolutely legendary.

This use is very common but slightly weaker than the full meaning of the word. It captures the spirit — something so good it deserves to be remembered — but without the full weight of enduring fame and historical significance. In casual contexts, it's perfectly fine and widely understood. In formal writing, it's better to reserve it for things that genuinely carry lasting greatness.

If something is legendary, it means it is so extraordinarily impressive, remarkable, or famous that it has entered the realm of stories — the kind people keep telling and retelling with admiration and awe. It may refer to figures from ancient folklore and myth, or to real people and events whose greatness is so massive that they feel almost mythical. Either way, the word carries a powerful sense of wonder, admiration, and lasting significance.
